For a plain 1.5% C steel this gives 224 + 1488 - 1046 = 666^\circ\mathrm{C}, below \mathrm{A_1}, which is impossible: Acm must rise above 727^\circ\mathrm{C} as carbon rises. 1.html:
Suggested treatment: spheroidising anneal, preceded by normalising to break the cementite network.

Microstructural features of the 1.5% C steel (as rolled or annealed)

  • By the lever rule, proeutectoid cementite = (1.5 - 0.8)/(6.67 - 0.8) \approx 12\%; the rest is pearlite. Total cementite = (1.5 - 0.025)/(6.67 - 0.025) \approx 22\%.
  • The proeutectoid cementite lies as a thick, continuous network on the prior-austenite grain boundaries; slow cooling or annealing makes it thicker.
  • Inside, lamellar pearlite: hard, brittle cementite plates alternating with ferrite.

Why this machines badly on a shaper. A shaper cuts with a single-point tool at low speed and re-enters the work at every stroke, so the edge takes an impact each time. The hard network and the lamellae abrade and chip the edge, raise the cutting force and tear the surface; tool life is short and the finish poor. Even coarse pearlite is too hard to machine conveniently (slide 12).

Why spheroidite helps. Spheroidising turns all cementite, lamellae and network fragments alike, into separate globules in a continuous soft ferrite matrix. The tool now shears ductile ferrite and pushes the isolated particles aside: maximum softness and ductility, the lowest cutting force and the best tool life for high-carbon steel. The driving force is the drop in ferrite-cementite interface energy: lamellae fragment, the pieces form particles, and the particles round off by carbon diffusion (slide 13).

Schedule

  1. Normalise above Acm (about 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} for 1.5% C), soak, air cool. The network dissolves and air cooling leaves fine pearlite with only thin, broken cementite. Fine pearlite spheroidises faster.
  2. Spheroidise by one of: holding just below \mathrm{A_1} (about 700^\circ\mathrm{C}) for 15 to 25 h; heating just above \mathrm{A_1} (about 740 to 760^\circ\mathrm{C}) then very slow cooling or holding just below \mathrm{A_1}; or cycling above and below \mathrm{A_1} (8 to 12 h cycles, slide 13). Then furnace cool.

Full annealing alone would leave coarse pearlite and a thicker network; normalising alone gives harder fine pearlite. Spheroidite is also the best starting structure for later hardening.
pts: Recommends a spheroidising anneal, preceded by normalising to break the network
Describes the steel: about 12% proeutectoid cementite as a continuous grain-boundary network plus pearlite (about 22% cementite in all)
Explains why that structure machines badly on a shaper: hard brittle cementite abrades and chips the single-point tool at each stroke, high force, poor finish
Explains spheroidite: globular cementite in a continuous ferrite matrix gives minimum hardness, maximum ductility and best machinability
Gives the mechanism: interface-energy reduction; fragmentation, particles, spheroids by diffusion
Normalising step: above Acm, air cool, dissolves the network, fine pearlite spheroidises faster
Spheroidising options: below A1 for 15 to 25 h; just above A1 with slow cooling or a hold below A1; cycling about A1
Explains why full annealing or normalising alone is not suitable

10a.html:
In Fe-C the eutectoid lies at 727^\circ\mathrm{C} and 0.76% C. Dissolved alloying elements change the relative stability of austenite and ferrite and the carbon solubility, so the eutectoid point moves (slide 79).

Eutectoid temperature

  • Austenite stabilisers Ni and Mn lower it by widening the \gamma field: about 610^\circ\mathrm{C} at 8% Ni and 670^\circ\mathrm{C} at 8% Mn. Enough of them keeps austenite stable at room temperature (Hadfield, 18-8 stainless).
  • Ferrite stabilisers raise it by shrinking the \gamma field, in the order Ti > Mo > W > Si > Cr: above 1200^\circ\mathrm{C} at 1% Ti, about 930^\circ\mathrm{C} at 4% Mo, only about 810^\circ\mathrm{C} at 6% Cr. A higher A_1 suits high-temperature service and tools, but heat-treatment temperatures must rise.

Eutectoid carbon

  • All elements lower it, since they reduce carbon solubility in austenite and carbide formers also tie up carbon. Ti is strongest (about 0.2% C at 0.5% Ti); Mo and W give about 0.2% C at 4 to 5%; Si, Cr and Mn give about 0.45 to 0.5% C at 4%; Ni is weakest (about 0.7% C at 4%).
  • Hence an alloy steel below 0.76% C can be eutectoid or hypereutectoid: a 5% Cr steel is eutectoid near 0.5% C, and a Ni steel holds more pearlite than a plain steel of equal carbon.

Ni and Mn (austenite stabilisers) lower the eutectoid temperature, with values or the austenitic-steel consequence
Ti, Mo, W, Si, Cr (ferrite stabilisers) raise it, with the order or values
All elements lower the eutectoid carbon; Ti, Mo, W strongest, Ni weakest, with values
Gives a consequence (hypereutectoid below 0.76% C, more pearlite, changed heat-treatment temperatures)

10b.fix: Slide 64 and page 160 of the course book say that in the second stage (200 to 300^\circ\mathrm{C}) retained austenite decomposes "to martensite". In carbon and low-alloy steels, retained austenite held at 200 to 300^\circ\mathrm{C} decomposes isothermally to bainite (ferrite + carbide); that is why stage 2 shows an expansion on a dilatometer. Retained austenite turns to fresh martensite only on cooling after high-temperature tempering (about 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}) of highly alloyed tool steels, which is a different process.

Key differences:

  • Stages 1 and 3 decompose martensite; stage 2 decomposes retained austenite, so it matters only in steels that retain austenite (above about 0.6% C).
  • The carbide changes from transition \varepsilon-carbide to equilibrium cementite, and in stage 4 it only coarsens and spheroidises (driven by lower interface energy).
  • In alloy steels, stage 4 also brings alloy-carbide precipitation (secondary hardening, about 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}).
  • The stages depend on time as well as temperature: for a eutectoid steel tempered 1 h (slide 65), about 61 HRC at 205^\circ\mathrm{C}, 56 at 315^\circ\mathrm{C}, 48 at 425^\circ\mathrm{C} and 39 at 535^\circ\mathrm{C}, each falling further with longer time.

Stage 3 (250 to 350 degrees C): \varepsilon-carbide replaced by cementite rods and films, matrix becomes ferrite; clear softening and tempered-martensite embrittlement
Stage 4 (above 350 degrees C): cementite coarsens and spheroidises, recovery then recrystallisation to equiaxed ferrite; alloy carbides in alloy steels

10c.html:
Tool steels contain several carbide formers, and each carbide has its own crystal structure: orthorhombic \mathrm{M_3C}, hexagonal \mathrm{M_7C_3} and \mathrm{M_2C}, complex FCC \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} and \mathrm{M_6C}, NaCl-type FCC MC. Four factors decide which forms:

  1. Atomic size ratio. If r_\mathrm{C}/r_\mathrm{M} < 0.59 (V, Mo, W, Ti, Nb: about 0.52 to 0.58), carbon fits the octahedral holes of a simple metal lattice: interstitial Group II carbides, MC (all holes filled) and \mathrm{M_2C} (half filled). Fe, Cr and Mn (about 0.61 or more) are too small, so complex Group I cells form: \mathrm{M_3C}, \mathrm{M_7C_3}, \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}, and \mathrm{M_6C} where W or Mo combine with Fe (slide 21 table).
  2. Composition. In the Fe-Cr-C system (slide 20), \mathrm{M_3C} forms in Cr-free high-carbon steel, \mathrm{M_7C_3} at high carbon and medium Cr, and \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} as Cr rises further. W and Mo give \mathrm{M_6C} and \mathrm{M_2C}; V gives MC.
  3. Kinetics. Carbon diffuses fast and substitutional atoms slowly, so \varepsilon-carbide and \mathrm{Fe_3C} form first in tempering. Cr then replaces Fe in it, and with time and temperature the carbide changes to \mathrm{M_7C_3} and then \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}.
  4. Stability. Elements left of Fe bond carbon more strongly; the most stable carbide wins with time, so the unstable ones (left end of each row in the slide 21 table) dissolve.
pts: Names the structures: \mathrm{M_3C} orthorhombic, \mathrm{M_7C_3} and \mathrm{M_2C} hexagonal, \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} and \mathrm{M_6C} complex FCC, MC NaCl type
Size ratio: below 0.59 (V, Mo, W, Ti, Nb) simple interstitial MC and \mathrm{M_2C} (Group II); Fe, Cr, Mn above it give complex Group I carbides
Composition: with rising Cr, \mathrm{M_3C} to \mathrm{M_7C_3} to \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}; W and Mo give \mathrm{M_6C} and \mathrm{M_2C}; V gives MC
Kinetics: fast carbon and slow substitutional diffusion, so \mathrm{Fe_3C} forms first and Cr gradually replaces Fe
Stability: stronger carbide formers make more stable carbides, which replace the unstable ones with time

11a.html:
Martensitic stainless steels are Fe-Cr-C alloys (11.5 to 18% Cr, 0.1 to 1.2% C), for example 410, 420, 431 and 440C. They are hardened like carbon steels, so the composition must give full austenite at the hardening temperature.

Preparation (heat treatment route)

  1. Anneal for machining: 750 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, 2 to 4 h, furnace or air cool; ferrite + carbides, about 160 HB (410).
  2. Preheat at 550 to 800^\circ\mathrm{C} (low thermal conductivity), protected against decarburisation.
  3. Austenitise at 950 to 1100^\circ\mathrm{C} to dissolve the carbides; more Cr and C need the higher end.
  4. Quench in oil (avoids grain-boundary carbides) or air (complex shapes): ferrite + carbide formation is so sluggish that sections up to about 300 mm harden in air. Martempering is possible. For 410, M_s \approx 350^\circ\mathrm{C}, M_f \approx 250^\circ\mathrm{C}; both fall with C.
  5. Subzero at about -75^\circ\mathrm{C} straight after hardening for high-C grades (retained austenite).
  6. Double temper. As-quenched hardness: about 35 HRC at 0.1% C, 60 HRC at 0.5% C.

Role of alloying elements

  • Cr: passive film and corrosion resistance; ferrite former that shrinks the \gamma loop; very high hardenability; carbides for wear (440C).
  • C: expands the \gamma loop (13% Cr needs over 0.15% C, 17% Cr over 0.3% C); sets martensite hardness (YS up to about 1900 MPa); lowers toughness, ties Cr in carbides and lowers M_s.
  • Ni (up to 5%): expands \gamma, prevents \delta-ferrite (17% Cr, 0.2% C needs 2% Ni: 431), allows lower C for toughness and corrosion resistance; too much leaves martensite incomplete.
  • Mo (up to 1%): corrosion resistance, toughness, tempering resistance; shrinks \gamma.
  • N expands \gamma; V forms fine carbides for wear and grain refinement (knife grade).

Effect of tempering (slide 29 figure, a hardened martensitic grade)

11b.html:
Duplex stainless steel (2205: 22% Cr, 5% Ni, 3% Mo, 0.15% N, 0.03% C) has about 50% ferrite (\alpha) and 50% austenite (\gamma). Each property follows from that structure.

How the structure forms. It solidifies as ferrite; austenite nucleates near 1300^\circ\mathrm{C} at ferrite boundaries, then inside the grains. Hot working at 1000 to 1200^\circ\mathrm{C} gives alternating \alpha/\gamma lamellae. Solution annealing at about 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} and water quenching fix the 50/50 balance (minor phase never below 30%). Cr, Mo and Si partition to ferrite; Ni and N to austenite.

Structure to property

  1. Strength: fine two-phase grains (each phase limits the other's growth), Cr-Mo-Si solid solution in ferrite and N in austenite give YS about 450 MPa against 280 MPa for 304, about twice; thinner walls save cost.
  2. Ductility and toughness: the FCC austenite deforms by dimpled fracture and arrests cleavage cracks, so toughness beats ferritic and martensitic grades.
  3. Chloride SCC: cracks are blocked at \alpha/\gamma boundaries, and ferrite resists chloride SCC.
  4. Pitting and intergranular corrosion: high Cr, Mo and N (PREN 33 to 43); C is low, and Cr diffuses fast in ferrite, so depleted zones heal.
  5. Cost: only about 5% Ni.
  6. Anisotropy: rolled lamellae make properties directional.

Structure-related limits. Ferrite is the weak point:

  • Sigma, chi, \mathrm{Cr_2N} and \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} form at 600 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} (within minutes), raising hardness, lowering toughness and draining Cr and Mo.
  • Cr-rich \alpha' at 350 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} (475 C embrittlement) causes ferrite cleavage, so service is limited to about 250^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  • Ferrite gives a ductile-brittle transition, and weld zones turn ferrite-rich unless Ni- and N-rich filler and a solution anneal are used.
pts: Describes the structure: about 50/50 ferrite and austenite, with typical composition (high Cr, Mo, N, low Ni and C)

Lower Ni gives lower cost; lamellae give anisotropy

12d.html:
An alloy is precipitation hardenable only if a fine second-phase dispersion can be produced from a single phase at will; the phase diagram shows whether this is possible.

Test 1: a sloping solvus. The solid solubility of the solute must fall with temperature. Al-Cu: Cu in \alpha-Al is 5.65% at the eutectic (548^\circ\mathrm{C}) but only about 0.1% at room temperature, so \theta (\mathrm{CuAl_2}) precipitates on cooling.

Test 2: composition inside the window. The alloy must lie between the room-temperature solubility and the maximum solubility, so that it is single phase above the solvus and two phase below. Al-4% Cu is all \alpha between the solvus (about 500^\circ\mathrm{C}) and 548^\circ\mathrm{C}, so it is solution treated at about 515 to 540^\circ\mathrm{C}. Al-10% Cu keeps eutectic, and Cu-Ni (complete solubility) has no solvus: neither can be hardened this way.

Test 3: enough precipitate. A steeper solvus gives more precipitate. Lever rule at room temperature for Al-4% Cu (\theta \approx 53.5\% Cu):

f_\theta = \frac{4 - 0.1}{53.5 - 0.1} \approx 0.07

Test 4: kinetics and coherency (not on the diagram). A quench must retain the supersaturated solid solution, and aging must form fine coherent clusters (GP zones, \theta'', \theta') whose misfit strain pins dislocations. An incoherent phase only at grain boundaries gives little hardening.

Stainless steels. In 17-4 PH, Cu dissolves at 1040^\circ\mathrm{C} but is almost insoluble in martensite at 480 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C}: the same sloping-solvus condition.

Confirmation: solution treat, quench, age; a hardness peak with aging time proves age hardening.

Criterion: composition within the window, single phase above the solvus and two phase below; solution treatment between solvus and eutectic

Counter-examples: no solvus (Cu-Ni) or composition beyond maximum solubility
Lever rule shows the amount of precipitate available (about 7% theta for Al-4% Cu)

2.html:
No. P is harmful in some structural steels and useful in others; the answer depends on the product, its carbon content, its heat treatment and its service.

Where P is harmful

  • Cold shortness: P segregates to grain boundaries, lowers their cohesion and raises the DBTT; brittle fracture becomes intergranular instead of transgranular cleavage.
  • Temper embrittlement: in quenched and tempered low-alloy steels P (helped by Mn and Ni, opposed by Mo) segregates to prior-austenite boundaries during tempering through about 375 to 575^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  • Processing: above 0.04% P galvanised coatings are rough and brittle; reheated deep-drawn sheet suffers secondary work embrittlement; welds crack more easily.

Hence the limits are customised: at most 0.02% for embrittlement-prone HSLA steels (Mn, Si, Ti, Nb, V, Cr), below 0.01% for low and moderately high (about 400^\circ\mathrm{C}) temperature service, while 0.02 to 0.03% is tolerated in low-strength grades and concrete rebar not exposed to hostile environments.

Where P is beneficial

  • Strength with formability: P is the most potent solid-solution strengthener of ferrite; 0.17% P raises the YS and UTS of low-carbon sheet by about 62 MPa. Being substitutional, it also improves bake hardening and deep drawability, so rephosphorised and P-added IF sheet (about 0.05 to 0.12% P) gives thinner, lighter car-body panels.
  • Atmospheric corrosion: weathering structural steel for bridges, railway wagons and unpainted buildings carries 0.05 to 0.15% P with 0.2 to 0.5% Cu, which form a dense, adherent rust layer.
  • Machinability and electrical use: P embrittles chips in free-cutting steels, and 0.10 to 0.155% P in cold-rolled motor-lamination steel lowers AC core loss. P also raises hardenability.

Conditions for safe use: low carbon, thin sections not quenched and tempered, about 10 ppm B to strengthen grain boundaries, and no long holds in the embrittling range.

Conclusion: P is detrimental in heat-treated, thick, welded or low-temperature structural steels, but a cheap and effective alloying element in sheet, weathering and free-cutting steels. It is not absolutely detrimental.

3.html:
How hardening takes place

  1. Austenitise. Heat to about A_3 + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C} (hypoeutectoid) or A_1 + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C} (hypereutectoid) and soak. BCC ferrite dissolves at most 0.022% C, but FCC austenite dissolves up to 2.14%: its octahedral holes (0.414R \approx 0.053 nm) are far larger than those of BCC (0.154R \approx 0.019 nm) for a carbon atom of 0.077 nm.
  2. Quench faster than the critical cooling rate. The cooling curve misses the pearlite and bainite nose, so carbon has no time to diffuse out and form ferrite and cementite.
  3. Shear below M_s. The FCC lattice changes to BCC by a diffusionless, cooperative shear. The carbon stays trapped in octahedral sites along one axis, stretching the cell into body-centred tetragonal martensite, c/a \approx 1 + 0.045(\%\mathrm{C}). The reaction is athermal: the amount depends on how far the steel is cooled below M_s, and it ends at M_f.
  4. Why it is hard. The supersaturated carbon distorts the lattice and pins dislocations; the shear leaves a dense dislocation (or twin) substructure and very fine laths or plates; the volume rises and internal stresses are high. Hardness therefore rises with dissolved carbon: \mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} = 35 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}), about 55 HRC at 0.4% C.
  5. Temper at once to relieve stresses and restore toughness.

Why austenitic stainless steel cannot be hardened

  • About 18% Cr with 8% Ni (plus Mn, N) makes austenite stable from solidification to below room temperature. There is no \gamma \rightleftharpoons \alpha change and no A_1 or A_3, so heating creates no new phase and quenching only keeps austenite.
  • M_s lies far below room temperature, about -165^\circ\mathrm{C} for 18Cr-8Ni (Eichelman-Hull), so quenching to room temperature makes no martensite.
  • Carbon is very low (0.08% maximum), and carbide precipitation is avoided because it sensitises the steel (425 to 815^\circ\mathrm{C}), so there is no precipitation hardening either.
  • Quenching from 1050 to 1100^\circ\mathrm{C} is solution annealing: it dissolves carbides and softens the steel.

They are strengthened only by cold working: work hardening, plus strain-induced martensite in metastable grades such as 301 and 304.

4.html:
Why full austenitising lowers M_s and the martensite fraction

  1. More carbon and alloy in solution. A high-carbon steel hardened just above A_1 keeps undissolved cementite, so its austenite holds only the carbon on the A_{cm} line at that temperature. Full austenitising above A_{cm} dissolves all carbides: the austenite takes the whole carbon content and the dissolved Cr, Mo and V.
  2. M_s is set mainly by dissolved carbon (slide 49):
M_s = 520 - 320\,\%\mathrm{C} - 50\,\%\mathrm{Mn} - 30\,\%\mathrm{Cr} - 20\,\%(\mathrm{Ni} + \mathrm{Mo}) - 5\,\%(\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{Si})

Each extra 0.1% C in solution lowers M_s by about 32^\circ\mathrm{C}; dissolved alloy lowers it further.

  1. Martensite forms athermally: the amount depends on how far below M_s the steel is cooled, not on time. With a lower M_s, M_f falls below room temperature and the M_s to M_f range narrows, so a quench to room temperature leaves more retained austenite.

Evidence. Slide 41: hardened from 845, 925 and 1040^\circ\mathrm{C}, M_s falls from about 230 to 130 to 90^\circ\mathrm{C} and the martensite at 20^\circ\mathrm{C} from about 98 to 80 to 50%. For a 1.2% C steel at 780^\circ\mathrm{C} the austenite holds about 0.93% C (M_s \approx 220^\circ\mathrm{C}); above A_{cm} \approx 860^\circ\mathrm{C} it holds 1.2% C (M_s \approx 136^\circ\mathrm{C}). With f_M = 1 - \exp[-0.011(M_s - 20)] the martensite falls from about 89 to 72%.

Change in M_s of the alloyed 1050

Given: 1050 taken as 0.50% C and 0.75% Mn; additions 3.0% Cr, 1.0% Ni, 0.6% Cu.

\begin{aligned} M_s(1050) &= 520 - 320(0.50) - 50(0.75) = 322.5^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \Delta M_s &= -30(3.0) - 20(1.0) - 5(0.6) = -90 - 20 - 3 = -113^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ M_s(\text{alloyed}) &= 322.5 - 113 \approx 210^\circ\mathrm{C} \end{aligned}

Cross-check with the per-element table of slide 49 (data for 0.8 to 1.0% C): -35(3.0) - 26(1.0) - 7(0.6) = -135^\circ\mathrm{C}. This is an upper limit, because alloying elements act more weakly at lower carbon, so the formula value is used.

Answer: M_s falls by about 113^\circ\mathrm{C}, from about 320 to about 210^\circ\mathrm{C}. The martensite at room temperature drops from about 96 to 88%, so the alloyed steel retains about 12% austenite.

Readings from the figure: nose about 0.75 s at 540^\circ\mathrm{C}; M_s \approx 220, M_{50} \approx 165, M_{90} \approx 130^\circ\mathrm{C}. At 300^\circ\mathrm{C} bainite starts at about 70 s, reaches 50% (dashed curve) at about 450 s and ends at about 2000 s.

Plan: stop the bainite reaction at 50%, then turn 80% of the remaining austenite (40 of the 50%) into martensite and keep the rest.

  1. Heating (assumed 0.80 C, 0.75 Mn, 0.25 Si): \mathrm{CE} = 0.80 + 0.75/5 + (0.25 - 0.5)/5 = 0.90 > 0.7, very crack sensitive. Heat slowly through 250 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} and preheat at 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Austenitise at about 780^\circ\mathrm{C} (A_1 + 50). Soak t = 60 + D = 60 + 152 \approx 212 min (about 3.5 h) in a protective atmosphere.
  3. Quench into an agitated salt bath at 300^\circ\mathrm{C}, faster than
\frac{727 - 540}{0.75} \approx 250^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}},

so the path misses the nose and no pearlite forms.

  1. Hold at 300^\circ\mathrm{C} for about 450 s (7.5 min), timed from reaching bath temperature: 50% lower bainite (above M_s, below about 350^\circ\mathrm{C}).
  2. Transfer within about 10 s (bainite still grows at about 0.14% per second) into hot oil at about 140^\circ\mathrm{C}. Interpolating between the M_{50} and M_{90} lines, 80% of this austenite has transformed at 166 - 0.75(166 - 130) \approx 139^\circ\mathrm{C}: 40% martensite.
  3. Hold at 140^\circ\mathrm{C} for 15 to 30 min, then cool slowly in air. Isothermal holding stabilises the remaining austenite (slide 41), so about 10% stays retained.
  4. Temper at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}, below 200^\circ\mathrm{C} where retained austenite starts to decompose.

Section-size check: the core of a 6 in (152 mm) plain-carbon bar cools at only a few ^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}, far below 250, and slide 68 limits austempering to 0.008 to 0.150 in sections. The schedule gives this structure only in a thin surface layer; the core becomes fine pearlite. For the full section a deep-hardening Ni-Cr-Mo steel (for example 4340) is needed.

6.html:
Why oil for intricate shapes

Thick and thin sections, corners, holes and keyways cool at different rates (slide 62), so martensite forms at different times in different places; that mismatch causes distortion and cracks. The ideal quenchant is fast through stages A and B, to pass the nose, and slow in stage C, where martensite forms, so stresses can equalise.

  • Water boils at 100^\circ\mathrm{C}, so fast nucleate boiling lasts until the steel is below about 150^\circ\mathrm{C}. Most steels form martensite above that, so they transform under the most severe cooling with large surface-centre and thin-thick differences. Water suits simple shapes and low-hardenability steels.
  • Oil boils over about 230 to 480^\circ\mathrm{C}, so its slow convection stage starts sooner, near or above M_s. Surface and core transform more nearly together and transformation stresses relax. Its severity is lower (H \approx 0.25 to 0.30 for still oil against 1.0 for still water, slide 26), and hot oil, being less viscous, breaks the vapour blanket evenly.

So oil gives less distortion and fewer quench cracks, and is used for intricate shapes and high-hardenability alloy steels.

Stress states in the figure

Outward arrows mean expansion, inward arrows contraction; solid circle surface, dashed circle centre.

  • (a) Uniformly heated: surface and centre both expanded; no stress.
  • (b) Start of quench: the surface cools and contracts first, the centre does not. Surface in tension, centre in compression; the hot austenite yields.
  • (c) Midway: the surface passes M_s and becomes martensite, less dense than austenite, so it expands while the austenitic centre still contracts. Surface in compression, centre in tension.
  • (d) Near the end: the surface is cold, rigid martensite; the centre now transforms and expands against it. Surface pulled into tension, centre compressed: this residual tension distorts the part and opens quench cracks in the brittle case.

Each 100^\circ\mathrm{C} of surface-centre difference means \sigma = E\alpha\Delta T \approx (200\ \mathrm{GPa})(1.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}})(100\ \mathrm{K}) = 240 MPa. Oil keeps \Delta T small during (c) and (d); martempering removes it.

7.html:
Challenges in hardenability control

High-carbon (0.75 to 1.10% C) high-alloy steels, such as bearing and tool steels and carburised cases, are hardened from 800 to 930^\circ\mathrm{C}, inside the austenite + carbide field. Their hardenability is therefore not fixed by the composition alone:

  1. Undissolved carbides. Only part of the carbon and alloy dissolves, and only the dissolved part raises hardenability and martensite hardness. The amount varies with austenitising temperature and time.
  2. Carbides nucleate pearlite. Undissolved particles start pearlite early on cooling and lower hardenability; their size, shape and distribution matter more than grain size.
  3. Prior microstructure. Normalised or quenched structures (fine, lamellar carbides) dissolve easily but supply many nuclei; spheroidised structures dissolve less but their few large spheroids are poor nuclei, so up to about 855^\circ\mathrm{C} they give the higher hardenability.
  4. No standard factors. Grossmann's low and medium carbon factors assume full solution; separate factors are needed, and one must find whether pearlite or bainite limits hardenability.
  5. Narrow temperature window. A higher temperature dissolves more carbon and alloy, but lowers M_s and M_f, leaving retained austenite (lower hardness), coarse grains and cracking risk; for 100Cr6 the 900 HV peak is reached only in a narrow range.

Hence strict control of prior structure, austenitising temperature and time is needed to reproduce hardenability.

Carbon needed for 60 HRC, 100% martensite

Given: 100% martensite, 60 HRC.

Find: the carbon content needed.

Solution: for (practically) 100% martensite use the 99.9% line of slide 22, \mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} = 35 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}):

\begin{aligned} 60 &= 35 + 50(\%\mathrm{C}) \\ \%\mathrm{C} &= \frac{60 - 35}{50} = 0.50 \end{aligned}

Answer: at least 0.50% C dissolved in the austenite, within the 0.6% C linear range. In a high-carbon high-alloy steel the extra carbon stays as carbides for wear; the austenitising treatment must put 0.50% C into solution without leaving retained austenite.

8.html:
How S and Mn act together (slide 4; book p 294)

  • S alone: S is almost insoluble in solid iron and stays in the melt as FeS or MnS. FeS promotes cementite, giving chilled, mottled or white iron.
  • Mn and S: Mn has a higher affinity for S than Fe has. MnS (or complex Mn-Fe sulphide) starts to separate early and keeps forming through freezing, so it is randomly distributed as harmless particles. Mn therefore first removes FeS: in a high-S, low-Mn iron, adding Mn reduces the chill.
  • Free Mn: only Mn beyond that needed for MnS acts on the structure. It resists graphitisation and stabilises pearlite.
Mn, wt%Microstructural effect
1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}stoichiometric MnS, no effect on the structure
1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15maximum ferrite, minimum pearlite
3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35pearlitic matrix

For 0.10% S, a ferritic iron needs about 0.32% Mn and a pearlitic one about 0.65% Mn. In ductile iron the S must be below about 0.02% before Mg treatment; Mg removes the rest, so all the Mn is free and is kept low.

Temper embrittlement: yes, it can be controlled (slide 16; book pp 306-307)

What it is. Quench-hardened ductile iron high in Si and P, tempered at 350 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} and cooled slowly, loses fracture toughness while its normal tensile properties stay unchanged. It also occurs when the matrix is tempered to full ferrite. P segregates to the grain boundaries during the hold or the slow cool and weakens them.

Control:

  1. Composition: keep P as low as possible and Si no higher than the grade needs. As in steels, Mn and Si assist P segregation, so do not exceed the Mn that the S rule requires.
  2. Mo addition: up to 0.15% Mo prevents it; Mo holds P and hinders its segregation.
  3. Heat treatment: avoid long holds in 350 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}, or cool quickly (oil or water) from the tempering temperature through that range.
  4. Recovery: the embrittlement is reversible. Reheating above about 600^\circ\mathrm{C} and cooling quickly restores the toughness.

9a.html:
Vacuum (low-pressure) carburising

Gas carburising in an oxygen-free chamber at low pressure, with a single hydrocarbon (methane, propane or acetylene) and no carrier gas.

  1. Load and evacuate the sealed furnace, removing oxygen and moisture.
  2. Heat under vacuum (a little \mathrm{N_2} aids convection) to 900 to 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} and equalise.
  3. Boost: admit the hydrocarbon in short pulses at 0.75 to 7.5 torr (about 1 to 10 mbar). It dissociates on the hot surface, for example \mathrm{C_3H_8 \rightarrow 3C + 4H_2}, and the high carbon flow brings the surface near saturation (about 1.3% C) within minutes; the pumps remove the hydrogen.
  4. Diffuse: gas off; carbon moves inward and the surface carbon falls.
  5. Repeat boost and diffusion steps, ending with a diffusion step that sets the surface carbon.
  6. Quench from the hardening temperature in high-pressure gas (\mathrm{N_2} or He) or oil; temper.

Features: no surface or grain-boundary oxidation; higher temperature and surface carbon shorten the cycle (slide 9: at 2 h the case at 1040^\circ\mathrm{C} is about 2.4 times that of gas carburising at 950^\circ\mathrm{C}); uniform case even in holes; minimum distortion; clean, green, automatic. Against: high capital cost, fine-grained steel needed above about 980^\circ\mathrm{C}, soot if overdosed.

Propane instead of methane (slide 10)

GasCarbon contentCarbon yield
Methane \mathrm{CH_4}75%below 3%
Propane \mathrm{C_3H_8}82%about 25%
  • Methane is the most stable hydrocarbon; at low pressure it hardly reacts on the steel, so the carbon flux is small, boosts are long and most gas passes unused. It needs higher pressure or a plasma.
  • Propane cracks readily: three carbon atoms per molecule and, per kg of gas, roughly 0.82 \times 0.25 / (0.75 \times 0.03) \approx 9 times more carbon delivered. Boosts are shorter, cycles faster and gas use lower.
  • But propane also cracks in the gas phase to methane, ethylene and tars, so soot and tar deposit on the load, furnace and pumps unless pressure, flow and pulse length are controlled. Acetylene (about 60% yield) is better still.
pts: Defines vacuum carburising: oxygen-free, low-pressure, single-hydrocarbon atmosphere without carrier gas
Steps: evacuate, heat to about 900 to 1050 degrees C, equalise
Boost pulses at about 1 to 10 mbar, dissociation on the surface to near 1.3% C, diffusion steps, repeated, final diffusion
Gas (or oil) quench and temper
Features: no oxidation, faster cycles, uniform case, minimum distortion, green; limits: cost, grain growth above about 980 degrees C, soot
Propane against methane data: carbon content 82% against 75%, carbon yield about 25% against below 3%
Consequence: much higher carbon flux, shorter boosts, less gas; methane needs higher pressure or plasma
Drawback: propane gives more soot and tar; acetylene is better

9a.watch:
• Carbon content is the mass fraction of carbon in the molecule (12/16 = 75%, 36/44 = 82%); carbon yield is the fraction that ends up in the steel.
  • The book says propane dissociates "100%" once heated; the 25% yield is lower because much of its carbon leaves as stable methane, tar or soot.
  • The case-depth ratio is read from the slide 9 graph.

9b.fix: Slide 22 says that above 490^\circ\mathrm{C} the gamma phase forms and nitrogen solubility falls (book p 202: "gamma prime phase temperature at 490^\circ\mathrm{C}"). On the Fe-N diagram on the same slide, 490^\circ\mathrm{C} is only the Curie (magnetic) temperature of \gamma'-Fe4N. Austenite appears only above the Fe-N eutectoid at 590^\circ\mathrm{C} (2.35% N). Nitriding at 495 to 565^\circ\mathrm{C} is therefore ferritic, as slide 21 says ("no phase change").
9b.html:
Surface hardness comes from fine, coherent alloy nitrides (AlN, CrN, VN) in the diffusion zone. HV against time gives a family of curves (sketch):

  • Lower temperature (about 500 to 525^\circ\mathrm{C}): nitrides stay fine; hardness is highest (about 1000 HV in an Al nitralloy) and nearly constant with time, which only deepens the case (d \propto \sqrt{t}).
  • Higher temperature (550 to 590^\circ\mathrm{C}): faster diffusion, but the nitrides coarsen (overageing) and the core tempers, so hardness falls faster and further with time.

Use the lowest temperature that gives the depth, below 590^\circ\mathrm{C}.
pts: Sketch of HV against nitriding time with curves for rising temperature: flat and high at low temperature, lower and falling at high temperature
Hardness comes from fine coherent alloy nitrides in the diffusion zone
Low temperature: maximum hardness kept with time; time mainly deepens the case (\sqrt{t})
High temperature: nitride coarsening and core tempering lower the hardness, which falls further with time
Conclusion: lowest temperature that gives the depth, below 590 degrees C

9c.html:
Both are selective hardening methods: the surface layer is austenitised and turned to martensite with no change of composition, so the steel needs at least about 0.3% C.

FeatureInductionLaser
Heat sourceeddy currents induced by high-frequency AC in a water-cooled Cu coil; heat generated inside the steelbeam absorbed at the surface; heat conducted inward
Depth controlfrequency, \delta = 5.03\sqrt{\rho/\mu f} cm, plus power and time; about 0.5 to 10 mmpower density, spot size, scan speed; about 0.1 to 1.5 mm
Heating timeabout 1 to 10 sunder 1 s
Quenchwater or polymer sprayself-quench into the cold mass
Hardness profilegradual, wide transition zonesharp drop, narrow transition, finer martensite
Distortion, oxidationlowlowest
Geometrycoil must fit the part; symmetrical partsany local area in line of sight
Cost, outputmoderate equipment, high mass productionhigh capital, low consumables, flexible

Critical issues, induction:

  • Frequency choice for the case depth; \delta jumps above the Curie point (\mu \to 1).
  • Coil shape and coupling gap: holes, slots and edges concentrate current, overheat and crack.
  • Power density against time: too high overheats or melts corners; too low soaks heat in and deepens the case.
  • Quench delay and uniformity (cracking of high-carbon or alloy steels); temper afterwards.

Critical issues, laser:

  • Absorption depends on wavelength, surface condition and angle; bright steel reflects much of a CO2 beam, so absorbent coatings are used.
  • Narrow window between transformation and melting: a slight error in power or time melts the surface.
  • Self-quench needs enough cold mass behind the track; thin sections and edges overheat.
  • Overlapping tracks back-temper the previous track into soft bands; spot shape and beam mode fix the zone shape.
pts: Heat source: eddy currents generated inside the steel by a coil, against surface absorption of a laser beam
Depth control: frequency through \delta (about 0.5 to 10 mm) against power density, spot and scan speed (about 0.1 to 1.5 mm)
Heating time of seconds against under a second
External spray quench against self-quenching
Gradual profile with a wide transition zone against a sharp profile with finer martensite
Geometry, distortion and cost or throughput compared
Induction issues: frequency, coil design and coupling, overheating at holes and edges, quench delay and cracking
Laser issues: absorptivity and coatings, narrow window before melting, enough mass to self-quench, back-tempering of overlapped tracks

9c.watch:
• "Discuss critical issues for both": give at least three issues for each process, each with its consequence.
